vision.purpose: BWS4 is an **overall framework and collection of example apps**, all built with Spec4, designed to give developers evaluating Spec4 concrete example apps demonstrating its capabilities for building agentic applications, and to educate users generally about different patterns and styles of using agents and AI in applications. Although presented as separate 'example apps,' they are all part of one unified BWS4 application.
vision.ui_surface: Web app (browser-based) — one unified application presenting multiple example apps
target_audience: Developers evaluating Spec4 for their own projects (primary)
Developers learning agentic AI patterns generally (primary)
The Spec4 team/maintainers, as a showcase for Spec4 itself (secondary)
Educators/students learning about agentic AI (secondary, possible)

Landing_Page.description: Introduces BWS4, explains that it and all example apps were built using Spec4, and lists the available example apps for users to explore.
Landing_Page.example: A single landing page acts as the entry point to all example apps within the unified BWS4 application.

RAG_Example_App.description: A single example app illustrating the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pattern, using a small, publicly downloadable dataset. Designed to be illustrative and educational rather than practically useful for a specific task.
RAG_Example_App.example: Demonstrates how retrieval and generation combine in an agentic workflow, using a small public dataset.

Shared_Framework_Services.description: Core services shared across all example apps, including LLM model/provider access (via LiteLLM and OpenRouter free models), a small local embedding model, a web search tool, and database access. These shared services run self-hosted on the project's netcup VPS alongside the web client, while the relational and vector store remains on Neon PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension. Because the instance is always on, the embedding model load and its 2D projection fit occur once at boot and stay warm for the lifetime of the process.
Shared_Framework_Services.example: Each example app draws on the same underlying LLM access, embedding, web search, and database services rather than reimplementing them — all served from a single always-on self-hosted instance.

Tool_Use_Integration.description: Example apps requiring tool use integrate with the free Exa search API.
Tool_Use_Integration.example: A tool-use example app calls Exa's free search API to retrieve real-time information.

Embeddings_Example_App.description: An example app illustrating the model embeddings pattern via a visual embedding explorer. A curated set of pre-configured text examples — a mix of word/short-phrase categories (e.g., animals, emotions, tech terms) and full sentences — are embedded using the framework's shared local embedding model, then projected to 2D and plotted so users can visually see semantic clustering. Users can also enter their own custom text, which is embedded and merged into the same recalculated 2D projection, rendered in a distinct color so it stands out from the pre-configured points. Includes a short educational overview explaining the embedding pattern. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps and is added to the landing page and hamburger menu. Must reuse the framework's existing shared embedding model rather than introducing a new one for this app.
Embeddings_Example_App.example: A user picks from pre-set examples across categories and sentences, sees them cluster by meaning in a 2D plot, then types their own sentence and watches it appear in a distinct color relative to the existing clusters.

Single_Call_Example_App.description: An example app illustrating the single-call pattern (per Spec4's pattern library tier 03: single_call) — one direct request to the LLM producing one direct response, with no retrieval, no tools, and no multi-step chaining. Users can enter a free-form prompt or choose from a set of preset example prompts (e.g., summarize, classify, extract). A toggle lets the user switch between Simple mode (plain text prompt → plain text response) and Structured mode (the request asks the LLM to return a JSON-schema-conforming response via structured-output prompting; both the structured request payload and the LLM's structured JSON response are displayed to the user). Includes a short educational overview explaining the single-call pattern and when it is appropriate. Uses only the framework's shared generation service (LiteLLM/OpenRouter) — no new services introduced. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps and is added to the landing page and hamburger menu.
Single_Call_Example_App.example: A user picks a preset prompt like 'classify this review,' toggles to Structured mode, and sees both the JSON request payload and the LLM's JSON-schema-conforming response rendered side by side with their plain prompt/response equivalent in Simple mode.

Chained_Calls_Example_App.description: An example app illustrating the chained calls pattern (per Spec4's pattern library tier 06: chained_calls) — a sequence of LLM calls where one model's output feeds into the next. Uses the framework's shared generation service and shared model/tool services, same as other examples. Includes a short educational overview explaining the chained calls pattern. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps and is added to the landing page and hamburger menu. IMPORTANT: To conserve model quota, this example is limited to exactly 2 chained model calls — the first call takes the initial user request, and its response is routed as input to the second call, which produces the final output. The UI/description makes clear this 2-call limit is a quota-conservation choice for this demo, and that the chained calls pattern itself supports any number of chained calls. Both the intermediate output (from the first call) and the final output (from the second call) are displayed to the user, and the user is told each agent's role upfront so they know what to expect.
Chained_Calls_Example_App.example: The user submits a story prompt (e.g., 'Tell me a story about a lighthouse keeper'). The first model call acts as a struggling writer and produces a short story based on the prompt — shown to the user. That story is then passed to the second model call, which acts as a very opinionated and harsh critic, producing a critique of the story — also shown to the user.

Planning_Agent_Example_App.description: An example app illustrating the planning agent pattern (per Spec4's pattern library tier 07: planning_agent) — a planner model call decomposes the user's goal into a plan of discrete steps, which are then carried out by separate executor model calls. The demo scenario is a trip-day planner: the user provides a city and their interests; a planner call produces a small plan (research steps using the framework's shared Exa web search tool, plus a final synthesis step that composes a one-day itinerary). The plan is displayed to the user first; the user then clicks a 'Next' button, which runs all executor steps in sequence, with each step's result displayed as it completes, ending with the final itinerary. Uses only the framework's shared model and tool services — no new services introduced. Includes a short educational overview explaining the planning agent pattern, which additionally cross-references the ReAct Loop example app as the interleaved counterpart to this app's plan-first approach: here the full plan is fixed and shown for approval before any step runs, whereas in ReAct Loop the model decides each next step only after observing the result of the previous one. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps and is added to the landing page and hamburger menu. IMPORTANT: To conserve model quota, each run is limited to a small fixed number of model calls (approximately 1 planner call plus 2–3 executor calls), and the user is limited to a small number of runs per session (exact number left to implementation). Both limits are clearly noted in the description, which also makes clear that in general a planning agent can use any number of agents/steps to accomplish its task.
Planning_Agent_Example_App.example: A user enters 'Lisbon' and 'food and history.' The planner call produces a plan: (1) research notable historical sites via web search, (2) research well-regarded local food spots via web search, (3) synthesize a one-day itinerary. The user reviews the plan and clicks 'Next'; the executor steps run in sequence, each result appearing as it completes, and the final itinerary is presented.

Orchestrated_Subagents_Example_App.description: An example app illustrating the orchestrated subagents pattern (per Spec4's pattern library tier 08: orchestrated_subagents) — a single orchestration agent receives the user's question, decides which specialists should handle it, delegates to them as independent subagents, and merges their results into one final answer. The orchestrator selects exactly two specialists from a fixed roster of four — Technical, Financial, Historical, and Practical — and first displays its delegation decision: which two specialists it chose, a short rationale for the pairing, and the specific brief (sub-question/instruction) it wrote for each specialist. The user then clicks a 'Next' button to dispatch. The two subagents run concurrently and are rendered as parallel columns with live per-subagent status, each column headed by that specialist's brief, so the fan-out and fan-in are visible on screen. When both subagents return, the orchestrator merges their answers into a single final response. Input is either a curated preset question — chosen to exercise different specialist pairings — or the user's own free-form question. The four specialists are knowledge-only with no tool access; the app uses only the framework's shared generation service and introduces no new services. Includes a short educational overview explaining the orchestrated subagents pattern and the demo, noting that subagents are independent workers that can run in parallel because neither depends on the other's output. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps and is added to the landing page and hamburger menu. IMPORTANT: To conserve model quota, this example uses exactly 1 orchestration agent and 2 subagents (3 model calls per run) and limits the user to 3 runs per session. A visible 'runs remaining' counter is shown on the page; once the runs are exhausted the input and 'Next' button are disabled with a clear explanatory message while previous results remain on screen, and the messaging distinguishes between hitting this app's 3-run session limit and hitting the shared daily framework usage cap. Both limits are clearly noted in the description, which also makes clear that in general the orchestrated subagents pattern can use any number of agents to accomplish its task.
Orchestrated_Subagents_Example_App.example: A user picks the preset question 'Should I buy or rent a home?' The orchestrator decides the question is best answered by the Financial and Practical specialists, explains why, and shows the brief it wrote for each. The user clicks 'Next'; the two specialists run side by side in parallel columns with live status, each answering its own brief, and the orchestrator then merges their two answers into a single final response.

Multi_Agent_Collaboration_Example_App.description: An example app illustrating the multi-agent collaboration pattern (per Spec4's pattern library tier 09: multi_agent_collaboration) — peer agents interacting as autonomous parties across a trust/ownership boundary, negotiating and exchanging work over a protocol such as A2A, rather than being workers controlled by a single owner as in orchestrated subagents. The demo scenario is competitive procurement with exactly 3 agents: a Buyer agent representing the visitor, plus two rival Seller agents owned by different (fictional) suppliers. Each seller holds private constraints — cost floor, stock level, delivery capability, support capacity — that neither the buyer nor the rival seller can see. The sellers compete on four deliberately non-comparable axes: price, delivery speed/lead time, quantity and partial fulfilment, and warranty terms, so the buyer must exercise judgment rather than pick a minimum. Input: the visitor selects a preset procurement scenario (each pre-tuned so the sellers' private constraints produce genuinely non-comparable bids) and sets a priority weighting (e.g., speed over price, full quantity required, longest warranty); there is no free-text input, and the same scenario can yield a different winner depending on the priorities chosen. Run flow — one negotiation round, exactly 6 model calls: (1) the RFQ is composed deterministically from the preset plus the visitor's priorities, with no model call; (2) the two sellers bid concurrently, blind to each other (2 calls); (3) the buyer reviews both bids and issues a targeted counter-offer to each seller (1 call); (4) the two sellers return best-and-final revised bids, still blind to each other (2 calls); (5) the buyer awards the deal with a rationale weighed against the visitor's stated priorities (1 call). Presentation: two parallel seller columns with live per-seller status (consistent with the Orchestrated Subagents app), plus a buyer track carrying the RFQ, the counter-offers, and the award; a private-position reveal at the end unseals each party's hidden constraints once the run completes, showing why a seller held firm or conceded; and an optional raw message-log toggle renders the same run as chronological sender-to-recipient protocol traffic, making visible that no message ever passes seller-to-seller. Protocol treatment is A2A-shaped and in-process: each agent publishes an inspectable Agent Card (name, provider, skills, capabilities), exchanges are structured A2A-style Task/Message/Artifact objects passed over an in-process message bus, and opacity is enforced in code rather than by prompt instruction so a peer can only ever see messages addressed to it; the overview states clearly that this uses A2A's data model and interaction pattern without the HTTP transport, and what a real deployment would add. Includes a short educational overview of the pattern and the demo, containing a candid note that all three agents ship in one BWS4 repo under one owner, that the trust boundary is staged for teaching purposes, and that the tier itself would treat this as over-engineering in a real system. Uses only the framework's shared model services — no new services introduced; the seller agents are knowledge-only with no tool access. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps and is added to the landing page and hamburger menu. IMPORTANT: To conserve model quota, this example uses a maximum of 3 agents and exactly 6 model calls per run, and limits user runs per hour at the framework's existing standard rather than a tightened per-app limit, with the shared hourly and daily usage caps backstopping total spend. The limits are clearly noted in the description, which also makes clear that in general the multi-agent collaboration pattern can use any number of agents to accomplish its task.
Multi_Agent_Collaboration_Example_App.example: A visitor picks the preset scenario '500 laptop docking stations, needed in two weeks' and sets their priority to 'speed over price.' The RFQ goes out to both sellers, who bid concurrently without seeing each other: one offers a fast delivery at a premium with a short warranty, the other a cheaper full-quantity bid on a longer lead time. The buyer counters each seller on its weakest axis; both return best-and-final bids — the manufacture-to-order seller cannot concede on delivery and holds firm. The buyer awards the deal to the faster supplier and explains why, given the visitor's stated priorities. The private-position panels then unseal, revealing each seller's true cost floor and stock level, and the visitor can toggle to the raw message log to see that no message ever travelled between the two sellers.

ReAct_Loop_Example_App.description: An example app labelled 'ReAct Loop' on the landing page and hamburger menu, illustrating the ReAct (Reason + Act) pattern — the interleaved reason–act–observe shape of the planning-agent tier (per Spec4's pattern library tier 07: planning_agent), presented in deliberate contrast with BWS4's existing plan-first Planning Agent example. The page opens with a short educational overview explaining the ReAct loop and how it differs from the Tool Use example (a single decision about whether to search) and from the Planning Agent example (a fixed plan approved before any step runs). The visitor chooses one of five curated multi-hop questions — questions whose answer requires chaining two or more facts, so a later search query can only be written after reading the earlier result — or types their own question, and starts the run. The five presets are: (1) 'How tall is the highest mountain in the country that most recently joined the United Nations?' (hop 1: most recent UN member, stable but not front-of-mind; hop 2: that country's highest mountain and its height, genuinely obscure); (2) 'Who is the current head coach of the national team that won the most recent FIFA Women's World Cup?' (hop 1: most recent tournament winner, time-variable; hop 2: that team's current head coach, volatile — both hops force search); (3) 'What is the population of the birthplace of the most recent Nobel laureate in Literature?' (hop 1: most recent laureate, refreshes every October, Literature chosen over Peace because the laureate is always an individual with a birthplace; hop 2: birthplace; hop 3: population — the one three-hop preset); (4) 'Which company currently employs the lead author of the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture?' (hop 1: paper and lead author, likely parametric; hop 2: current employer, has changed repeatedly and recently, reliably defeating memory); (5) 'What is the tallest building in the birthplace of the director of Spirited Away?' (hop 1: director and birthplace, likely parametric; hop 2: tallest building in that city, time-variable — the approachable pop-culture entry point). Preset selection criteria: every preset must require chaining at least two facts where the later query cannot be written until the earlier result is read, and must contain at least one hop that defeats parametric knowledge — either time-variable ('current' / 'most recent') or genuinely obscure — so the trace shows real observations doing real work. Presets store questions only, never answers, so time-variable answers self-refresh from search on every run and only an occasional sanity pass (does each question still parse, is the laureate an individual, etc.) is needed for maintenance. The app then fills a live trace, cycle by cycle: the model's short thought appears; then the action it chose — either the exact search query it issued to the framework's shared Exa web search tool, or its decision that it can now answer; then the observation — the result snippets the search returned; then the next thought, which visibly builds on what was just observed. No plan is shown up front and the visitor approves nothing mid-run — the model alone decides each next step, which is precisely the contrast with the Planning Agent example and is called out in the overview. The overview also notes that on presets 4 and 5 a model may state the first hop from its own knowledge in its thought and spend its searches on the hop that actually needs them: this is correct ReAct behaviour, and the trace showing the model choosing where observation is required is itself teaching content; presets 1-3 guarantee at least one demo where every hop visibly comes from an observation. Every run ends in one of two states, both shown candidly: a final answer card stating which observations the answer drew on, or — when the fixed cycle cap is reached before the model is confident — a budget-exhausted card presenting the partial trace and naming what remained unresolved, rather than dressing it up as an answer. Uses only the framework's shared generation and Exa web search services — no new services introduced. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps. IMPORTANT: To conserve model quota, each run is capped at approximately 8 search actions plus 1 final-answer call (roughly 9 model calls per run — a deliberately generous budget so the loop has runway and the budget-exhausted ending is rare, mostly reserved for hard free-form questions), and the visitor is limited to 2 runs per session, the tightest per-app limit in the gallery because this is the most expensive example per run. A live cycle counter (e.g. 'search 3 of 8') advances during the run so the visitor can see the budget being consumed and anticipate a budget-exhausted ending, and a visible 'runs remaining' indicator mirrors the Orchestrated Subagents app; once the runs are exhausted the input and start control are disabled with a clear explanatory message while previous results remain on screen, and the messaging distinguishes between hitting this app's 2-run session limit and hitting the shared framework usage cap. Both limits are clearly noted in the description, which also makes clear that ReAct agents in general run any number of cycles.
ReAct_Loop_Example_App.example: A visitor picks the preset 'What is the tallest building in the birthplace of the director of Spirited Away?' The first thought identifies Hayao Miyazaki as the director and notes that his birthplace needs confirming; the action issues a search, and the observation returns snippets naming Tokyo. The next thought builds on that observation — now that the city is known, it can ask which building is currently tallest there — and issues a second search; the observation returns snippets about Azabudai Hills Mori JP Tower. The model then decides it can answer, and the final answer card names the two observations it drew on. The cycle counter shows only 2 of 8 searches were needed, and the runs-remaining indicator drops to 1.

Self_Hosted_Deployment.description: BWS4 is deployed as a single always-on self-hosted instance on a netcup VPS 500 G12 (2 vCores, 4 GB DDR5 ECC RAM, 128 GB NVMe). Both the backend and the built web client are served from that VPS behind a public HTTPS origin with a valid certificate; PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension remains external on Neon. The previous host (Render) is retired entirely. Because the instance is always on, the embedding-model load and the 2D projection fit happen once at boot and stay warm, eliminating the cold-start delay visitors previously experienced on first visit, and the 4 GB of guaranteed RAM removes the memory pressure that made the previous host's free tier unusable. The migration is deliberately behaviour-preserving: no example app changes, no usage caps change, and no visitor-facing messaging changes — the gallery behaves exactly as before, simply faster and always warm.
Self_Hosted_Deployment.example: A visitor opens the BWS4 landing page over HTTPS and the first example app responds immediately, with no spin-up wait, because the backend, the web client, and the warm embedding model are all running continuously on the project's own VPS while the database continues to be served from Neon.

Router_Example_App.description: An example app labelled 'Router' on the landing page and hamburger menu, illustrating the routing pattern — a cheap classification call decides which of several existing paths should handle a request, after which code dispatches to that path and the model that made the decision gets out of the way. Routing is not a tier in Spec4's pattern library and this app does not claim one: the decision is tier 03 (single_call) — exactly one model call returning a typed object, i.e. a single call with the structured_outputs mechanism attached — and everything after it is deterministic dispatch to paths whose tiers are already cited; there is no new rung for the composition. The page opens with a short educational overview explaining routing: why a request should be answered by the cheapest path that can answer it well, why the decision is a separate small call rather than a capability of a bigger one, and how routing differs from the Tool Use example (the router emits a label and stops and never sees the result, whereas in Tool Use one model decides whether to call a tool inside its own turn) and from the Planning Agent and ReAct Loop examples (no step follows the dispatch, whereas in those apps one model keeps control across several steps). The overview also states that the router's scores are the model's uncalibrated self-report and that the one calibrated number on the page is the measured agreement rate with expected routes. The router chooses among exactly four existing routes: (1) a no-model deterministic evaluator — a real expression parser over an allow-list of operators and units covering basic arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷, parentheses, percentages) and conversions within three unit families (length, speed, temperature), which never executes model-produced text; (2) a single call through the shared generation service; (3) the RAG example's existing retriever over its space-exploration dataset; and (4) the shared Exa web search followed by one generation call. The router is told each route in one line: the deterministic route's line lists its supported operations and unit families, generated from the same table the evaluator's validator checks against, and the RAG route's line carries the subject list derived at startup from the document titles the retriever actually indexes (currently Apollo 11, Sputnik 1, the Space Shuttle, the ISS, Hubble, JWST, Curiosity and SpaceX). The page shows these route descriptions byte for byte as the router received them, together with the fixed decision margin printed next to them. Input: the visitor chooses one of six curated requests or types their own. Each preset carries an expected route and a one-line reason, and stores the request only, never an answer: (1) 'Convert 72 km/h to metres per second.' — expected route deterministic; reason: a pure calculation within the evaluator's scope that needs no model; control for the conversion pair. (2) 'Rewrite "hey, can u send me the report asap" so it sounds professional.' — expected route single call; reason: needs language generation but no outside facts. (3) 'How long did Apollo 11 spend on the lunar surface, and who stayed in orbit?' — expected route RAG; reason: answerable from the Apollo 11 document in the dataset; control for the space pair. (4) 'Who won the most recent Formula 1 race?' — expected route search plus generation; reason: a time-variable fact that neither the model's memory nor the dataset can be trusted to hold. (5) 'When is the next crewed launch to the International Space Station?' — expected route search plus generation; reason: near-miss — the subject is in the dataset but the answer is time-variable. (6) 'Explain why 1 mile is about 1.609 kilometres.' — expected route single call; reason: near-miss — it looks like a unit conversion but asks for an explanation, not a calculation. Presets 1 and 6 form the conversion control/near-miss pair and presets 3 and 5 form the space control/near-miss pair. The router returns a score for each of the four routes, plus a structured expression if it scores the deterministic route highest. The app first shows the routing decision as a structured decision card: the chosen route, a one-line rationale, all four scores on every run (so the visitor can see how close a confident decision was), and — for presets — a plain statement of whether the router agreed with the expected route, saying 'misrouted' when the router chose a different route and 'declined' when it did not choose. For free-text requests there is no expected route, and the card says only what was decided and why. A run takes the low-confidence path when the top two scores are within a fixed margin set in code; those two routes are, by construction, the routes the router was torn between, and the run dispatches to the cheaper of the two in a fixed cost order defined in code (deterministic, then single call, then RAG, then search plus generation), with the caveat shown on the card. The app then dispatches using the gallery's existing machinery and shows that path's answer in the same layout the corresponding example app uses, labelled with which path produced it. If the router's chosen route is deterministic, code validates the structured expression against the evaluator before anything is released; if the evaluator cannot compute it, the request is dispatched to single call with the reserved unit still held, and the decision card states plainly that the route was deterministic, the evaluator could not compute the expression, and the request was dispatched to single call — a misroute of the router's own making that is shown as such. If the low-confidence tie-break lands on deterministic and the evaluator rejects the expression, the request is dispatched to the other of the two routes it was torn between with the unit still held, and the low-confidence card states that the evaluator could not compute the expression; it remains the low-confidence ending because the router never chose. Alongside the answer sits a cost strip comparing the route actually taken against a 'no router' baseline — the heaviest path (Exa search plus one generation call) applied to every request — by resource type: model calls, searches, retrievals, and wall-clock time, with the router's own classification call shown separately as overhead. The route taken always shows its own measured time. The baseline's wall-clock time is always labelled 'typical' and never presented as this run's time; it is the rolling median of real search-route runs across all visitors, kept in the existing database so it survives restarts, and the strip states the sample size it rests on. Before that history holds at least five observations, the baseline is shown as counts only, with a note that typical latency appears once enough search-route runs have been observed; no hard-coded nominal figure is ever shown. When the router chose the search route, the strip says plainly that routing added one call and saved nothing on this request. The agreed/disagreed/declined history: after each preset run the outcome is recorded in the existing database, and the page shows, per preset, the counts agreed, disagreed and declined, with an overall rate shown above them; each rate is agreed divided by all three counts, and each cell shows counts only until it has at least five observations. Free-text runs and comparison re-runs feed no cell, and a tie-break that happens to land on the expected route earns no credit. Comparison re-run: whenever a preset run's dispatched route differs from its expected route — whether the router chose wrongly or declined and the tie-break landed wrong — the visitor may re-run the request once through the expected route. The router does not run again; the original decision card and misrouted answer stay on screen and the re-run answer appears beside it, labelled with its path, with a cost strip showing the route's own spend against the same no-router baseline and the router overhead shown as an explicit zero. The re-run counts as one of the visitor's five runs, reserves only the expected route's dispatch cost, and never feeds the latency or agreement history, because it is a forced route and not a routing outcome. If the tie-break landed on the expected route, no re-run is offered, and free-text requests get none. Every run ends in exactly one of two candidly presented states: a routed answer with its decision card and cost strip (including the evaluator-fallback correction), or a low-confidence decision card that names the two routes it was torn between and dispatches to the cheaper of them with that caveat shown. A refusal because the shared cap is too close is not an ending state; it is a run that never began. Uses only the framework's shared generation and Exa web search services, the RAG example's existing retriever and dataset, and the existing database for the two histories — no new services, datasets or providers are introduced. Follows the same overall layout as the other example apps. IMPORTANT: To conserve model quota, each run costs at most 2 model-call units (the router's call included) — 1 on the deterministic route, 2 on the others, plus one Exa search on the search route — making this the cheapest example in the gallery, and the visitor is limited to 5 runs per session, with a visible 'runs remaining' counter; before the router runs, 2 units are reserved against the shared generation cap, and the second is released only once the evaluator has accepted the expression, so a run that cannot finish is never started. Once the runs are exhausted the input and run controls are disabled with a clear explanatory message while previous results remain on screen, and the messaging distinguishes between hitting this app's 5-run session limit and hitting the shared framework usage cap. Both limits are clearly noted in the description, which also makes clear that routers in general can choose among any number of paths.
Router_Example_App.example: A visitor picks preset 5, 'When is the next crewed launch to the International Space Station?' The router scores the four routes; the decision card shows search plus generation scoring highest, with RAG a distant second because the ISS is in the dataset, and states that the router agreed with the expected route. The search is issued, one generation call composes the answer, and the answer appears in the Tool Use layout labelled as produced by the search path. The cost strip shows the route taken matches the no-router baseline in counts (1 search, 1 generation call), adds the router's classification call as overhead, says plainly that routing saved nothing on this request, shows this run's measured time next to the 'typical' search-path time with its sample size, and the runs-remaining counter drops to 4. The visitor then picks preset 1, 'Convert 72 km/h to metres per second.' The evaluator accepts the expression and answers in milliseconds with no generation call; the strip shows one unit spent and the second released, set against the baseline's search and generation call. The per-preset agreement table updates beneath.

differentiators: Built entirely with Spec4 itself — BWS4 is a living, dogfooding demonstration of the tool it promotes, not just documentation or tutorials about it.

monetization.current: Free, non-monetized project — exists purely for education and demonstration purposes.

Additional_Example_Apps.description: Expand the collection of example apps to cover additional agentic patterns and styles beyond RAG, tool-use, embeddings, single call, chained calls, planning agent, orchestrated subagents, multi-agent collaboration, and ReAct.
Additional_Example_Apps.example: Human-in-the-loop, MCP, parallel fanout, reflection, retrieval reranking, structured outputs, tool agent.

constraints: Must be hosted on a netcup VPS 500 G12 (2 vCores, 4 GB DDR5 ECC RAM, 128 GB NVMe, always-on), which serves both the backend and the web client; PostgreSQL with pgvector remains external on Neon.

The existing environment contract must carry over to the new host unchanged — model provider credentials, the Exa web search credential, a single non-wildcard allowed browser origin for the API, and optional error tracking — and secrets must never be committed to the repository.
The public origin must be served over HTTPS with a valid certificate.
The hosting migration must be behaviour-preserving: no example app behaviour changes, no usage cap changes, and no visitor-facing messaging changes.
Must use LiteLLM to access only free LLMs provided by OpenRouter.
The Embeddings example app must reuse the framework's existing shared embedding model rather than introducing a new or separate embedding model.
The Single Call example app must use only the framework's shared generation service, introducing no new services.

The Chained Calls example app must be limited to exactly 2 model calls to conserve model quota, while the description/UI must make clear that the chained calls pattern generally supports any number of chained calls.

The Planning Agent example app must limit model calls per run to a small fixed number (approximately 1 planner call plus 2-3 executor calls) and limit the user to a small number of runs per session, with both limits clearly communicated in the description, while making clear that planning agents in general can use any number of agents/steps.
The Planning Agent example app's educational overview must cross-reference the ReAct Loop example app as the interleaved counterpart to its own plan-first approach.

The Orchestrated Subagents example app must use exactly 1 orchestration agent and 2 subagents (3 model calls per run) and must limit the user to 3 runs per session, with both limits clearly communicated in the description, while making clear that the orchestrated subagents pattern in general can use any number of agents.
The Orchestrated Subagents example app must use only the framework's shared generation service and introduce no new services; its four specialist subagents are knowledge-only with no tool access.

The Multi-Agent Collaboration example app must include no more than 3 agents (1 buyer plus 2 sellers) and exactly 6 model calls per run, and must limit user runs per hour following the framework's existing standard practice, with both limits clearly communicated in the description, while making clear that the multi-agent collaboration pattern in general can use any number of agents.
The Multi-Agent Collaboration example app must use only the framework's shared model services and introduce no new services; its two seller agents are knowledge-only with no tool access.
The Multi-Agent Collaboration example app's RFQ must be composed deterministically from the preset scenario and the visitor's priority weighting, with no model call, to conserve quota.

The Multi-Agent Collaboration example app must enforce peer opacity in code rather than by prompt instruction — each agent can only see messages addressed to it, and no message may pass directly between the two seller agents.

The Multi-Agent Collaboration example app implements A2A's data model and interaction pattern (Agent Cards, Task/Message/Artifact) over an in-process message bus, without the HTTP transport; the educational overview must state this plainly and note what a real deployment would add.

The Multi-Agent Collaboration example app's educational overview must include a candid note that all three agents ship in one BWS4 repo under one owner, that the trust boundary is staged for teaching purposes, and that the tier itself would treat this as over-engineering in a real system.
The ReAct Loop example app must use only the framework's shared generation and Exa web search services, introducing no new services.

The ReAct Loop example app must cap each run at approximately 8 search actions plus 1 final-answer call (roughly 9 model calls) and must limit the visitor to 2 runs per session, with both limits clearly communicated in the description, while making clear that ReAct agents in general run any number of cycles.

The ReAct Loop example app must show a live cycle counter during a run and a 'runs remaining' indicator, disabling input once the session runs are exhausted while leaving previous results on screen, and must distinguish in its messaging between this app's 2-run session limit and the shared framework usage cap.
The ReAct Loop example app must show no plan up front and must require no visitor approval mid-run — the model alone decides each next step.

The ReAct Loop example app must end every run in one of exactly two candidly presented states: a final answer card naming which observations the answer drew on, or a budget-exhausted card presenting the partial trace and naming what remained unresolved.

The ReAct Loop example app's curated presets must store questions only and never store answers; every preset must require chaining at least two facts where a later search query cannot be written until the earlier result is read, and must include at least one hop that defeats parametric knowledge (time-variable or genuinely obscure).

The Router example app's routing decision must be exactly one structured model call (a single call returning a typed object with a score for each of the four routes), after which code — not the model — dispatches to the chosen route; the router never sees the result of the route it chose, and no further model step follows the dispatch other than the route's own generation call.

The Router example app must offer exactly four routes — the deterministic evaluator, a single call, the RAG example's existing retriever, and Exa web search followed by one generation call — and must use only the framework's shared generation and Exa web search services, the RAG example's existing retriever and dataset, and the existing database for its two histories, introducing no new services, datasets or providers.

The Router example app must limit the visitor to 5 runs per session, with a visible 'runs remaining' counter; each run must reserve 2 units against the shared generation cap before the router runs and release the second unit only once the evaluator has accepted the expression on the deterministic route, so a run that cannot finish is never started; a comparison re-run counts as one of the five runs; and the messaging must distinguish this app's 5-run session limit from the shared framework usage cap, disabling input when runs are exhausted while leaving previous results on screen.

The Router example app must end every run in exactly one of two candidly presented states — a routed answer with its decision card and cost strip, or a low-confidence decision card that names the two routes it was torn between and dispatches to the cheaper of them with that caveat shown — and a refusal before a run begins must not count as an ending state; an evaluator-fallback must be stated on the decision card within whichever of the two states the run is in, and must never be presented as the low-confidence state when the router chose confidently.

The Router example app's low-confidence rule must be decided in code: the run is low-confidence when the top two of the four model-reported scores are within a fixed margin printed on the page; the two routes named as torn between must be taken from those scores rather than from a separate runner-up claim; the cheaper of the two must be chosen by a fixed cost order defined in code (deterministic, single call, RAG, search plus generation); and the decision card must show all four scores on every run.

The Router example app's curated presets must store requests only and never answers, and every preset must carry an expected route and a one-line reason that states why that route is the right home for it, so a later reader can judge whether a disagreement is the router's fault or the preset's; the six presets must include two control/near-miss pairs (conversion wording and space wording).

The Router example app's deterministic evaluator must be a real expression parser over an allow-list of operators and units — basic arithmetic, percentages, and length, speed and temperature conversions — and must never use eval or otherwise execute model-produced text; the supported-operations line given to the router must be generated from the same table the validator checks against so the two cannot drift; and an expression the validator rejects must fall back to single call (or to the other tied route in the low-confidence case) with the reserved unit still held.

The Router example app must show the router's route descriptions on the page byte for byte as the router received them, with the RAG route's subject list derived at startup from the document titles the retriever actually indexes rather than written by hand, and with the fixed decision margin printed beside them.

The Router example app's cost strip must compare the route taken against a 'no router' baseline of Exa search plus one generation call, by resource type (model calls, searches, retrievals, wall-clock time), with the router's classification call shown separately as overhead; the route taken must always show its own measured time; the baseline's wall-clock time must always be labelled 'typical', never presented as this run's time, drawn from the rolling median of real search-route runs across all visitors stored in the existing database, shown with its sample size, and shown as counts only until at least 5 observations exist, with no hard-coded nominal figure; and when the search route is chosen the strip must say plainly that routing added one call and saved nothing on this request.

The Router example app's comparison re-run must be offered only for preset runs whose dispatched route differs from the expected route, never for free-text requests; must reserve only the expected route's dispatch cost without running the router; must show the router overhead as an explicit zero rather than omitting the row; must display beside the original answer and decision card; and must never feed the latency history or the agreement history.

The Router example app's agreement rate must be kept per preset from shared history in the existing database, with an overall rate shown above the six presets, and report agreed, disagreed and declined counts per preset, with the rate computed as agreed divided by all three; each cell must show counts only until it has at least 5 observations; free-text runs and comparison re-runs must be excluded from every cell; and a low-confidence tie-break that happens to match the expected route must earn no credit.

The Router example app's educational overview must state that the router's scores are the model's uncalibrated self-report and that the calibrated number on the page is the measured agreement rate with expected routes, and must state plainly that routing is not a tier in Spec4's pattern library — the decision is a single call (tier 03) with the structured_outputs mechanism attached, and everything after it is deterministic dispatch to paths whose tiers are already cited.

The Router example app must call the existing single-call, RAG and web-search paths through their existing service entry points without modifying them; its own code (router, evaluator, dispatch, cost strip, histories) must be new and fully lint- and type-checked and placed outside every extend-exclude path; nothing may be added to the exclusion list; and any change that proves unavoidable inside an excluded file must be kept to the minimum and flagged in the plan as touching excluded code.

revision_history.goal: Add a new Embeddings example app to BWS4 that visually demonstrates the model embeddings pattern using the framework's shared embedding model.
revision_history.rationale: Embeddings is a well-defined pattern tier in the Spec4 pattern library and was previously listed only as a future example; this revision implements it now as a visual, educational explorer reusing existing shared framework services, consistent with how RAG and Tool-Use were built.

revision_history.goal: Add a new Single Call example app to BWS4 that demonstrates the single-call agentic pattern, including both simple text and structured (schema-conforming) response modes.
revision_history.rationale: Single call is a well-defined foundational tier in Spec4's pattern library and was not yet represented among BWS4's example apps; this revision implements it as an educational demonstration reusing only the framework's shared generation service, and additionally showcases structured-output prompting by letting users toggle between simple text and schema-constrained JSON responses.

revision_history.goal: Add a new Chained Calls example app to BWS4 that demonstrates the chained-calls agentic pattern via two role-played, sequential LLM calls, while conserving model quota.
revision_history.rationale: Chained calls is a well-defined tier in Spec4's pattern library and was not yet represented among BWS4's example apps; this revision implements it as an educational, quota-conscious demo where a 'struggling writer' agent generates a short story and a 'harsh critic' agent critiques it, capped at exactly 2 chained model calls while making clear the pattern generally supports any number of chained calls.

revision_history.goal: Add a new Planning Agent example app to BWS4 that demonstrates the planning agent pattern via a trip-day planner scenario, with user-triggered execution and strict quota conservation.
revision_history.rationale: Planning agent is a well-defined tier in Spec4's pattern library and was not yet represented among BWS4's example apps; this revision implements it as an educational, quota-conscious demo where a planner call decomposes a trip request into a plan shown to the user, who then triggers the executor steps (web-search research plus final itinerary synthesis) with a single 'Next' click, capped by a small per-run call count and per-session run limit while making clear the pattern generally supports any number of agents/steps.

revision_history.goal: Add a new Orchestrated Subagents example app to BWS4 that demonstrates the orchestrated subagents pattern via an orchestrator that chooses two specialists from a fixed roster, briefs them, runs them concurrently, and merges their answers — under strict quota conservation.
revision_history.rationale: Orchestrated subagents is a well-defined tier in Spec4's pattern library and was not yet represented among BWS4's example apps; this revision implements it as an educational, quota-conscious demo where the delegation decision and per-subagent briefs are made visible and two independent specialists run in parallel columns, capped at 1 orchestrator plus 2 subagents and 3 runs per session while making clear the pattern generally supports any number of agents.

revision_history.goal: Add a new Multi-Agent Collaboration example app to BWS4 that demonstrates the multi-agent collaboration pattern via a competitive procurement negotiation between a buyer agent and two rival seller agents holding private constraints, exchanging A2A-shaped messages across a code-enforced opacity boundary — under strict quota conservation.
revision_history.rationale: Multi-agent collaboration is a well-defined tier in Spec4's pattern library and was not yet represented among BWS4's example apps; this revision implements it as an educational, quota-conscious demo in which two independently-owned seller agents bid and counter-bid blind to each other across price, delivery, quantity and warranty, and the buyer agent awards the deal against the visitor's own stated priorities — with A2A Agent Cards and Task/Message/Artifact exchanges over an in-process bus, opacity enforced in code, private positions revealed at the end, and a candid note that the trust boundary is staged for teaching since the tier itself warns this pattern is commonly over-reached.

revision_history.goal: Add a new ReAct Loop example app to BWS4 demonstrating the interleaved reason-act-observe shape of the planning-agent tier, in deliberate contrast with the existing plan-first Planning Agent example, and cross-reference the two apps from the Planning Agent overview.
revision_history.rationale: ReAct is the canonical interleaved counterpart to the plan-first decomposition already demonstrated by BWS4's Planning Agent app, and showing both under the same tier teaches the distinction that matters most in practice: whether the plan is fixed up front or discovered one observation at a time. The curated multi-hop presets guarantee that a later search query can only be written after reading the earlier result, so the trace shows real observations doing real work, and the candid budget-exhausted ending teaches that an unresolved run is a legitimate outcome rather than something to disguise.

revision_history.goal: Migrate BWS4's hosting from Render to a self-hosted netcup VPS 500 G12, serving both the backend and the web client from the VPS behind an HTTPS origin while keeping PostgreSQL with pgvector on Neon.
revision_history.rationale: BWS4 outgrew Render's free tier on memory and has been running on a paid starter plan whose cold starts were the showcase's most visible rough edge; an always-on VPS with 4 GB of guaranteed RAM costs less, removes the memory ceiling, and keeps the embedding model and 2D projection warm from boot. The migration is deliberately behaviour-preserving so no example app, usage cap, or visitor-facing message changes.

revision_history.goal: Implement the Router example app, which is already fully specified in the vision but was found by a code rescan to be not yet built.
revision_history.rationale: The code rescan shows no Router routes, capability or package, so the feature specified in the previous vision still needs to be built. This revision makes it new implementation work with its description unchanged.
